utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. May we have the -- could you call the case, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Muireann Dennehy on behalf of the Prosecution, along with my colleague Rachel Friedman, and the Case Manager, Thomas Laugel, with our intern Matija Saftic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You have a witness for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: I do, yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: No, I believe it's GH-119.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: No, there are no protective measures in place for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please give us your name, date of birth, and ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Milan Conjar. I was born on the 12th of October, 1963. And I am of Croatian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Conjar, you are about to make the solemn declaration, by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. So I need to tell you that you are exposing yourself to the -- the penalty of perjury should you give untruthful or misleading information to the Tribunal. Could you please read the solemn declaration now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Ms. Dennehy, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Conjar, are you able to hear me?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Conjar, do you recall giving a statement to the investigators of the Tribunal in 1996?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Turning to tab 2, can I please ask that the English version of 65 ter number 2238.1 be shown. This is dated 9 February 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Conjar, do you recognise the document on the screen in front of you to be the statement that you gave?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes, because I can see my signature at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you. And that was my next question, Mr. Conjar. So looking at the bottom of the first page, can you please confirm again that you recognise the signature in the bottom left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And before coming here today, did you have an opportunity to review a translation of this statement in your own language?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: You mean immediately prior to coming to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Yes, or while you were in The Hague, and prior to coming to court this morning.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes, I had an opportunity to have a good look at my statement, at the entire statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And if I were to ask you the same questions as you were asked in 1996, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: I certainly would. I probably would give the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And now that you have taken the solemn declaration, do you affirm the truthfulness and the accuracy of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: I stand by the statement that I gave on that day, on the 9th of February.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders the statement as 65 ter 2238.1, and asks that it be entered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would object because the witness said that he would probably give the same answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Dennehy.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Conjar, is there anything that you would like to change about this statement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And so if I can ask you again: Would you give the same answers as you gave in 1996, when you met the investigators of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Perhaps you're a bit confused because I said "probably." But I'm not sure if I would repeat what I said word for word. But I stand by the substance of what I said in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Your Honours, on that basis, the Prosecution would like to tender this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit Number P300. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: For ease of reference, I would like to -- that the witness be given a hard copy of his statement in his own language. Could the court usher please assist. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Conjar, I would now like to ask you a number of additional questions about the events described in your statement. At paragraph 3, you describe the attack on Lovas which took place on the 10th of October, 1991. Was the village shelled before that day?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: It was, on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And can you tell me when the village was shelled? What dates was the village shelled?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Well, it was on the 5th, the 3rd, and the 1st, prior to that date, and another occasion in the course of September. So in October before they entered the village, the 3rd, the 5th, and the 1st of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Were any religious buildings in Lovas damaged as a result of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes. The church of Saint Michael's that was destroyed on the 5th -- or, rather the bell tower was destroyed on the 5th. But it was hit before. It was destroyed on the 5th, but it had been damaged prior to that date.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: After the attack on Lovas, what armed forces were present in the village?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: I would say that the formations were paramilitary formations. Afterwards, regular JNA army units appeared.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And do you know the names of any of the paramilitary groups that were present in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Members of the Dusan Silni group.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And did you ever have occasion to meet any member of the Dusan Silni group?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And where did you meet a member of the Dusan Silni group?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: In my father-in-law's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what was the Dusan Silni doing in your father-in-law's house?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: They had found accommodation in my father-in-law's house. I don't know what they were doing there, while I wasn't present in the house, but I came across them. They were slaughtering a pig when I was there. They were doing this in the bathroom, in the bath, boiled the skin there.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: I would like to now turn to paragraph 8 of your statement where you mention Milan Devcic. What position did Milan Devcic hold in Lovas following the attack?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Milan Devcic was commander of the police or the commander of the police in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And when did he take the position of police commander in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can you please confirm whether it was before or after the attack on Lovas?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Before the attack on Lovas there was no police station in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: So, again, can you please tell us whether it was after the attack.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: After the attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: At paragraph 11 of your statement, you say that you went to the police station to report to Milan Devcic for work details. What do you mean by that term?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: What do I mean? Well, when I established contact with my parents after the attack, when my mother told me that Milan Devcic was asking about me, about the brothers, and said that I should return but nothing would happen to us, that we would have to work, I then reported to them, made myself available, in fact. I took him at his word. I believed that what he said he would do would be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And were you supervised while doing that work?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: On a daily basis. And I was under armed escort.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And were you paid for the work?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes, by having one additional day to live if we did what they ordered us to do. Only after some time had elapsed, we were given some sort of compensation in the form of coupons that we could use to buy one candle that would last for about one hour, no more than that, and that was the only form of compensation that we received for one day's work.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can you please describe the most difficult work that you were ordered to carry out?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: The most difficult work for me was collecting dead bodies. One day we received the order to collect a dead body which was near the graveyard by the road where there were plum trees, I believe. The body was in the grass. Our duty was to put the body in a nylon bag and bury it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And whose body was this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: It was the body of Rudolf Jonak.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And was Rudolf Jonak known to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Who ordered to you bury the body?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but we received orders in front of the building of the local office where the municipality is now located in Laso [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what was the municipality building that is now known by -- known as -- know by at the time, so in 1991, what was the building called?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: There was a room where weddings were held in that building, and the local committee Lovas was there; it had its office. And the post office was also part of the building, or in the building, and at the rear there was a flat.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And in 1991, what forces were stationed at that building?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Later the TO, the Territorial Defence, had its headquarters there.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now, moving on to paragraph 16 of your statement, you've provided evidence about Ljuban Devetak. What position did Ljuban Devetak hold in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Ljuban Devetak was the unofficial master of everything that went on in Lovas. He was the be-all and end-all in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Conjar, I would now like to show you a photograph that was -- appear on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Would the Court Officer please display 65 ter 6276. That's at tab 3 of the Court bundle. And this is an aerial photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Conjar, do you recognise the photograph in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what is this a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: This is a satellite photograph of Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: I can explain the photograph for you, if you like, because I use this sort of map in the course of my work almost every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can you please circle the house that was used as the police station by Milan Devcic on the photograph and mark it with the number 1.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: If we could zoom in a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And if you can just mark the number 1 next to that, please. And can you also indicate to the Trial Chamber the house that was used by Devetak.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Devetak lived in the flat across the road, in the building across the road. Shall I mark it with number 2? It was across the road from that building.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Yes, please, if you would.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I please ask that this 65 ter 6276 be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The one that is marked by the witness, you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document shall be marked with Exhibit Number P301. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Conjar, at paragraph 12 of your statement, you say that you were brought to the police station on two occasions by one of the men who had taken over your father-in-law's house. While there, you heard Ramiz Ferhatovic being beaten. Who was beating him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: I don't know who was beating him, but I heard the blows. I heard the groaning, the screaming from the cellar. The sound reached me in the room that I was in.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Was anyone else beaten at the police station?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: On that day when I was there?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: On that day or any other day that you are aware of.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that after this incident I was taken there for interrogation on one other occasion, and they beat up an elderly man - he was about 60 years old - before they got to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And do you know that man's name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: His name is Marko Gracanac, an elderly man.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Were there other locations in Lovas where people were being detained by those controlling the town after the attack?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes. There were several places.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber where those places were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: I can. The first place where people were detained was in the offices of the mechanical work-shops of the agricultural co-operative in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And who was detained at the mechanical work-shop?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: A large number of people. Some they had come across. Others had been collected from their houses and taken there.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And who was responsible for the detention at the Zadruga building, at the mechanical work-shop of the Zadruga building?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Was there anywhere else in Lovas that people were detained?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there was the building where the registry was located; it was across the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And who was detained at that building?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Well, they were detaining people there, people they had taken from their homes, and some of the people had been taken from areas outside the settlement itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: I would like to now move on to your detention at the Zadruga building. At paragraph 15 of your statement, you said that on the 17th of October, all men between the ages of 17 and 50 had to report to the community building at 5.00 p.m. Who ordered that all men were to go to the Zadruga building on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Ljuban Devetak.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: I would now like to show you another photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Would the Court Officer please display 65 ter 6277. That's at paragraph 4 of the Court's bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Conjar, do you recognise the building in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Was this the building where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can you please mark with the number 1 the mechanical work-shop that you just mentioned where there were others detained.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And can I ask that you now mark with the number 2 where you sat on benches for the evening of the 17th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And, finally, can I ask that you mark with the number 3 where the position of the machine-gun was pointing at you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I now please ask that this 65 ter 6277 be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The marked photograph under 65 ter 6277 shall be assigned Exhibit Number P302. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Conjar, can you please tell the Court what happened to you and the other men on the night of the 17th of October at the Zadruga building.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: From the very moment we entered the work-shop and after we were searched, we were ordered to line up and sit on the benches that -- that were parallel to the walls of the work-shop building. Across the room, a machine-gun was pointed at us. We were told that we would stay there the entire night, that we shouldn't move, that we should not talk. In the course of the night, we were visited by the guards. They daunted us, insulted us, ill-treated us. They took our names. They noted them.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: The following -- the following morning, you said that Ljuban Devetak, some paramilitaries, and members of the special forces arrived at that building and that beatings took place that morning. Can you please describe to the Court those beatings.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: It's very difficult to describe all the things that they did to the people who were there. They had a list. They read out 22 names from the list. As soon as a name was called, the person would have to run a gauntlet of people with rods, rifle-butts, batons, parts of machinery, hydraulic hoses and things like that. Whoever passed through the gauntlet would be hit either by a rifle-butt or a rod or would be kicked, and then if they fell down, they all swarmed upon him. They would continue beating him until they -- that person got up. And then they continued beating them. All the 22 men had to endure that and all the 22 had been terribly beaten. They suffered and -- and their sufferings are not easy to describe in words.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Your brother's name was called out that morning. Can you please describe what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: My brother had to run the same gauntlet, just like all the others whose names had been called up. He was a tall man, almost 2 metres tall, and he was beaten by metal rods. After that, he was never able to walk straight. The entire side of his body was probably cracked and fractured.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Conjar, I would now like to take you to the time that you were at the minefield. You said that after the first explosion, they started firing at you. Who started firing at you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Our escorts who took us to the minefield, they were behind us. Some of them were on the side of the road, standing in a line.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And who were those escorts? Who -- who were those men?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: It was a platoon of specials, a special unit from Valjevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Was there any reason for this special unit from Valjevo to fire at you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Nothing but execution.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: I'd now like to return to your brother. When you were laying in the minefield, you saw your brother-in-law's wife and your mother passing in an ambulance. Where were they going?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: A small correction: It was not an ambulance.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: You saw them passing in a vehicle. Where were they going?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes. There was, indeed, a vehicle, and my sister-in-law is -- was in it. She was nine months pregnant at the time. And there was another vehicle where my mother was. My sister-in-law was being taken to a hospital to give birth.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And when did she give birth?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: On the 20th of October. Two days after my brother was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And where was your brother killed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: In the minefield.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: That concludes my questions for now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Conjar. My name is Zoran Zivanovic, and in this case, I represent Goran Hadzic. Mr. Conjar, according to the information that I have, you provided previous statements, one of them to the Croatian judiciary bodies. I believe that that was in 2006. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Please jog my memory?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this: Do you remember that you ever provided the Croatian judicial bodies any kind of statement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: I provided several statements. I can't remember their chronological order. I don't know whether that was, indeed, in the year that you have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "several times," does that mean that you provided the Croatian bodies several statements about the events in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Not only Croatian bodies. When I left Lovas, from that moment until the statement that I provided in Belgrade, I provided several statements but I can't give you their chronological order. I can't tell you when I gave what statement. I would have to see what I stated, then I could confirm and I could answer your question. I would have to see the details of that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If need be, I'll show it to you. I just wanted you to tell us whether you provided statements. But you said you did.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: I don't remember. I can't tell you exactly what I said and when I said it. I can't answer your question, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in Belgrade before the Trial Chamber for War Crimes, there was a trial against Ljuban Devetak, Milan Devcic and a group of people who were tried for the crimes committed in Lovas in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You provided two statements, as far as I know, and if you want me to, I can show those statements to you. The first was given to an investigating judge --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes, I was there twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you the following. At the beginning of the crisis in the former Yugoslavia, what was your profession? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: I was not employed. I had a degree, a university degree, in agriculture.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you resided in Lovas; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe the situation in Lovas for us, up to the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Relatively calm, especially in view of what was going on around Lovas. Nothing significant was happening in Lovas, if you are alluding to interethnic problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, were you a member of a political party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What party was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: The Croatian Democratic Union, or the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether there was an HDZ board in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes. There was a Croatian Democratic Union board there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who were its members; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: I can assume that -- about some people, but I'm not a hundred per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: For example? Give us a name or two.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Mr. Jozo Milas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if Marko Gracanac was a member?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Marko Gracanac junior or senior?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Marko Gracanac named Markica.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Marko Gracanac junior, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: At that time, we know that Lovas had a majority Croatian population. Nearly 90 per cent of the population were Croats. In the HDZ party in Lovas, were there any Serbs as members?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes, there were. I can even give you a name of a lady who was a member. Branka Grkovic. She was a Serb and she was an HDZ member. I believer that there were others as well, but I'm sure that she was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In any case, do you agree with me that a vast majority of the HDZ members were Croats?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did it ever interest you why the Serbian population did not join the HDZ in Lovas in somewhat greater numbers?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Can you repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, did you ever try to find out, how come that the Serbian population in Lovas did not join the HDZ in greater numbers?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: I wasn't interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You were on good terms with the Serbs who lived in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes. My next-door neighbour was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that his name is Milan Miljkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: No. Milos Miljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I believe that you also had very close relations with Milan Devcic; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes. Milan Devcic was my best man at -- at my wedding.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss that issue with him? Did you ask him how come he did not join the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to him about possible objections to the HDZ policies that either he or other Serbs who resided in Lovas may have had?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: No, we never discussed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Conjar, we have come by a piece of information, according to which in 1990, sometime in late April, there was a meeting held in the village of Bogdanovci. A decision was taken at that meeting for the Croatian Democratic Union to become a military organisation. According to that same information, that decision was also implemented in Lovas. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to that same information, three services were established around that time. One of them was a technical service headed by Ivo Madzarevic; the other one was a military service headed by Markica Gracanac, and a medical service headed by Franjo Mujic and Branko Krizmanic. Are you familiar with these people?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes, I know these people. They are all villagers of Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to them at the time? Were you in communication with them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have also learnt that a volunteer detachment was set up in Lovas. Its commander was Markica Gracanac. It had 120 men as its members. Did you ever hear about that detachment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: No. This information takes me by surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have also learnt that in the village of Bogdanovci, there was a lineup of volunteer detachments and that the detachment from Lovas also took part. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the information that we have, those men from Lovas were transferred by buses and private cars. We're talking about a rather good organisation of people from such a small place as Lovas. Did you notice that transport taking place from Lovas to Bogdanovci?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to that same information, between 1500 and 2000 members of volunteer detachments from various places, including Lovas, attended that review of volunteer detachments in Bogdanovci.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. For your information, I can tell you that at the time my wife was pregnant. She had a complicated pregnancy. I was not employed. We had another older child, so I simply did not have the time to think about things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you take any steps in view of the fact that you were unemployed to find a job?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Of course I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, what steps did you take.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: I did everything I could. In Lovas at the time, I was temporarily employed by the football team as a janitor, which means that I mowed the football pitch that was -- that took six hours every day. I cleaned the premises after the games and training sessions. I also washed the tablecloths and other textiles, so I didn't have the time to follow those things that you asked me about. And, also, I worked temporarily on building walking trails around Lovas. I did the latter thing in the morning, and, in the afternoon, I worked on the football pitch in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And how long did that last for? How long did you work on -- at the football pitch?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Well, until the summer of 1991, effectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps then you could tell us something about another piece of information that I have. On the 29th of September, 1991, a football game was played in Lovas between the local team and the Sloga team from Borovo. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: On the 29th of September, 1991, no game was played.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. Let's go back to the beginning. As you searched for work, did you talk to Jozo Milas?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: I talked to Mr. Rendulic, the director of the agricultural co-operative in Lovas. He was in charge of employment there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what about Jozo Milas, did you talk to him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: I did not ask him for a job. I did talk to him but not about employment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did Jozo Milas promise you a job?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Not strictly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it conditional upon anything?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: No, there were no conditions attached to anything. But he suggested that I should join the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And if you did that, where would you be employed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: I assumed that he would offer me a job in my profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you assume that you would find employment in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Anywhere. Because I was unemployed and, as that was the case, I would have welcomed any job.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did Jozo Milas work at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Jozo Milas was a secretary, a lawyer in the Lovas agricultural co-operative.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will now quote you when you testified at the court in Belgrade with regard to this matter, or I will show you something about that. It is exhibit number 4 from the 65 ter list, 3189, page 59.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I would just inform the Trial Chamber that the whole document has not been translated yet and, unfortunately, this part of document is not translated. Our request is pending.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll read it out because it's very short. I think you can see it on the page. Page 59. Somewhere in the middle. You say in response to a question put to you by the lawyer Zdravko Krstic. The witness, Milan Conjar: Yes, Milos promised me that I would be employed if I joined the HDZ. It's in the Cyrillic script. I don't know whether you can read it easily.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes, I am sufficiently literate. I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember having said this before the court in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And is that, in fact, what you said, what it says here?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: He put this to me perhaps differently. Perhaps Mr. Krstic wanted me to say yes. But, in essence it is what you asked me about. He suggested that I join the HDZ. That was the proposal made and it was said that I would find employment then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time of the former SFRY, you didn't do your military service, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Then I've made a mistake. When the Crisis Staff was established in Lovas, did you have any duties that related to the defence of Lovas?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: I wasn't a member of the Crisis Staff. For a certain period of time, I did perform guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the purpose was of performing guard duty. What were you protecting Lovas from, and from whom?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: The purpose of performing guard duty was to prevent people or groups from entering the area, to ensure that no one acted in a disruptive manner in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And before these guards were established, were there any incidents in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: No. As far as I can remember, there were no incidents of any particular significance. Practically nothing. Apart from one, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did Serbs also stand guard?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes, there were Serbs too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will now ask you to have a look at page 72 of this same document. It is at the very beginning, at the top of the page. The question put to you by the lawyer, Igor Olujic, is as follows: "What I'm interested in," he says, "is whether the Serbs participated in the guards that were established within the framework of the Crisis Staff." And your answer was: "I do not know. I cannot remember."

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Well, then, that's the information I heard. There were no Serbs with me when I was on guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think you said that this is what you subsequently heard; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: After the trial in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you hear anything about the men who were involved in those guards?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll now move onto issues that concern your statement, and my learned friend from the Prosecution put some questions to you about it. What I'm interested in is when the attack was launched on Lovas by the JNA and the paramilitary formations, was any resistance mounted in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Organised resistance? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any unorganised resistance?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Perhaps a shot or two were fired by people who were fleeing, but there was no resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you have a younger brother whose name is Josip.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the trial in Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a look at the same document, in fact, page 80.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Dennehy.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: If I could have a moment, we don't have a translation of this document, nor is a translation available to the Trial Chamber. And while we have allowed some questioning on this issue, any further questions is quite difficult, given the lack of a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know why the Prosecution did not seek the translation of the whole document but just translation of the parts maybe most convenient for them, and we did it, but it requires time. It is documents from Rule 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So it's a Prosecution document, Ms. Dennehy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is from the Rule -- it is 3189 from the Prosecution list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm told -- I'm told that there are six partial English translations; in total about 30, 40, about 50 pages long, out of 92. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: I believe so, yes, Your Honour. However, there isn't a full translation of this document, and I believe the reason for that was time and resource constraints. But what I would object to is the further use of any parts of this document that there isn't a translation available for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think that would be rather unfair, wouldn't it? What -- what would be the remedy for the Defence? What would you suggest?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: My --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Or do you suggest just don't use it?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: The objection is based on the fact that there may not be a translation available in respect of any of the parts to which the Defence is referring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Translation is pending, we are told.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In that case, I withdraw my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may -- may just add. I used this document, this particular document, just to remind the witness. I'm not -- I not tender the whole document into evidence. It is not my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But you do confirm that the translation, at least from the parts that you are using now, is pending.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We were on page 80 of the transcript from the trial. You will find the part I'm interested in at the bottom. Slobodan Zivkovic put the question to you and he says: Very well. In your testimony of the 11th of March, 1996, Ante Luketic said that resistance was mounted by Jakob Balic, Sinisa Pavlicic, Tomo Balic, and certain others, as well as Josip Conjar. And then you puts a question to you, and you've answered that. Tell me, do you remember that question and your answer? You also said that your brother was mobilised into the Croatian Guards in the course of the war, in Osijek?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the next page now. At the bottom, where it says that in the course of the war your brother was in the guards in Osijek. It also says, or we can also find the following question and your answer. The lawyer Slobodan Zivkovic asks you the following again: Very well. You said that when there was this HDZ celebration in Lovas, you weren't present. You were at a football match. This was on the 29th of September, 1991. Did your brother also play football there? And your answer was: They were playing there, but the younger categories were playing.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: We're getting the dates mixed up again. The 29th of September, 1991. Perhaps there's a mistake in the date. 1991. It was perhaps in 1990. We didn't play football in 1991. The cup was no longer held. The last one was held in Pacetina on the 19th of June. The HDZ was established prior to that date, the 19th of June, 1991. The attack on Tovarnik was on the 20th/21st of September, 1991, and after the attack, no more matches were played. So perhaps there was a mistake in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, look, here you say that they were playing but it was the younger categories that were playing.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes. When my brothers were juniors, pioneers, they then played football, when they were 15 or 16. They played for the Lovas football club. And I continued to play actively up until 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And as can you see, it continues and the lawyer asks you who were you playing against there? And you replied, In Borovo Selo. Against whom? Against whom did you play? Against Sloga Borovo.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you provide some very characteristic details.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: The Sloga Borovo football club, I played against them at the time. That was the name of the football club from Borovo Selo, Borovo village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The only thing is that you provide answers within the context of questions about a football match played on the 29th of September, 1991. And that is why I'm asking you about this and I am dwelling on this football match, for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: I'm repeating what I said. On the 29th of September, 1991, no football matches were played. Perhaps there's a mistake in the transcript. This was perhaps a year earlier. When the HDZ celebration was held in Lovas, the Lovas football club played a match in Borovo Selo, Borovo village, against the Sloga Borovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When was this HDZ celebration in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: I would say -- well, I don't know what the exact date was. I know it was on a Sunday. We were playing a -- the match up until noon, from 10.00 to noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe this celebration? Were there any speeches?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: No. As I am saying, I was playing football while this was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned your neighbour. I think he lived - and still does live - right next to you, Milos Miljkovic, a Serb. In your statement you described in detail how the JNA attacked Lovas, and you described what was done on that occasion. Tell me, concerning the units that carried out the attack, the paramilitary formations and the JNA, did they throw a grenade into his house?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: No, not into the house but into the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why they did that? Why did they throw a grenade into his house?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: They didn't throw a grenade into his house. They threw a grenade into his cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, very well, the cellar is part of the house.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: No, the cellar is under the hill. The house is at the other end, on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that. Were grenades thrown into any other houses, apart from his house or, rather, into any other cellars?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes, a grenade was thrown into my brother's house and into certain other houses as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why they threw grenades into these cellars? Did you hear anything about this? Did they say anything about the matter?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Well, I know people would hide in their cellars. I was nearby. I heard when they were asking people to leave the cellar in Milos Miljkovic's yard. I heard people coming out. But they threw a grenade in just in case. This was in order to make sure that no one opened fire on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, they were afraid that when people were coming out of the cellar, someone might remain behind with a weapon and might then open fire on them.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: That's what I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like you to explain the detail of the event in the minefield, i.e., how Kraljevic, whose name was Ivica, Ivica Kraljevic, how did he get killed? Did you see the event? Did you see how that transpired? How did he get killed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: At the moment when we hit the mines in the minefield, the first person who did that stopped. All the rest of us were lined up in a straight line, and they ordered us to proceed, to continue walking into the minefield. The first step was made by Ivica. He was the one who said, I'll go first. He stepped out and, unfortunately, he activated a mine. Then fire was opened, so some people were killed by mines and the others were killed by bullets fired into their backs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you close to him when that happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Could you define the term "close"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you hear him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes, I could hear him really well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that you could also see him; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: It's not easy to see when you're lined up in a straight line. It's very hard to -- to see very far to the right and to the left, but I could hear his voice very clear and loud.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your vicinity, in the vicinity of that lineup, in his vicinity, was there a member of a military or a paramilitary formation; and, if there were, can you tell us how far were they from us [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: There were several of us behind our backs. They were members of the special police escort that escorted us, and there were two locals of Lovas among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How far from you were they? You were standing straight in front of the minefield. How far away behind you were they, according to your estimate?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Not more than 50 metres, up to 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did any of them approach you? Did they come closer to you; for example, a metre or 2 metres behind you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, I may be wrong to say this, but let's say that he decided himself to do what he did. Nobody pushed him intentionally or by mistake. Nobody pushed him into the minefield.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: What do you mean? Who would make their own decisions if threatened and if threatened with a gun?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying, but I want to exclude one possibility. Did somebody, for example, push him into the minefield when he hit the -- that mine?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying you don't know or is it the way you have just explained? Did you hear him say, I'll go first?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: He was the one who stepped out first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But did he utter those words, the words that you quoted: I will be the first.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: He says, I'll start. Maybe I am not rephrasing his words properly. He said, I'll be the first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So he announced his intention. Could you please answer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that's time for a break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, it's the time for our first break. We will come back at 11.00. The court usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Conjar, I would like to thank you for your answers. I have nothing further for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have finished my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Dennehy, re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I don't have any further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness Conjar, in today's transcript on page 4, we read, on lines 15 through 20, about the Church of Saint Michael's which was destroyed by shelling and the first thing that collapsed was the bell-tower and then that happened on -- in October 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you tell me what religion did this church belong to? What faith.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: It was a Catholic church.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Were there any other churches belonging to other religions in the village of Lovas?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Conjar --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- in cross-examination, you were asked the following: "According to our information, three services were established around that time. One of them was a technical service, headed by Ivo Madzarevic, the other was a military service headed by," I don't have the name, "and medical service headed by Franjo Mujic and Branko Krizmanic. Are you familiar with these people?" And your answer is: "Yes, I know these people. They are all villagers of Lovas." However, you were not asked whether you know of the existence of the three services that they allegedly headed, a technical, a medical and military service. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About their positions? No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: About the -- and about the existence of these three services.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CONJAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Conjar, this is the end of your testimony today. You are now released as a witness. We thank you very much for coming to The Hague to assist us, and we wish you a safe journey back home. The court usher will now escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Dennehy, after Ms. Clanton yesterday, today it was your turn to get on your feet for the first time in court.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Yes, it was, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I congratulate you for a job well done.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Do we have another witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The short answer, Your Honour, is perhaps. I haven't spoken to Defence counsel directly but I understand that there may be some issues if we were to advance the witness who was scheduled for tomorrow because we've -- we've finished a lot earlier than we thought we would, to bring him forward and start today, and I heard not directly from counsel but from my colleagues that perhaps this would be not suitable for -- for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we hear from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honours. I was informed that -- about the intent of the Prosecution to bring this witness today - he was scheduled for tomorrow - this morning, at 9.00. So I didn't finish my preparation for his examination or cross-examination and documents relevant for -- for his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: How long would examination-in-chief take, Ms. Biersay?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: We are currently down for two and a half hours, and I suspect we may go ten to 15 minutes longer than that. But two and a half is the current time. Perhaps it may be faster, but I doubt it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, do you have a problem with today's start only for examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. But I would ask the Trial Chamber to -- to let us submit our list for cross-examination later, not right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Would that suit? Would you agree to that, Ms. Biersay? So in that case we could start today and have the list for cross-examination by, let's say, tomorrow morning 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I think that is reasonable, Your Honour. If it's possible to have it earlier, that would be very good. And perhaps with the leave of the Court and with the agreement of counsel, we could have some extra time to review those documents tomorrow. But I don't think that should be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see how it goes and then we -- the witness is here?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: He is here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I believe he -- VWS, that they've brought them down in anticipation of this. And, once again, I apologise to the Court, I'll have to do some changes with my colleagues to prepare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Can the witness be brought in? Which witness is it, Ms. Biersay?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: This will be Witness GH-095.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Protective measures of pseudonym, Ms. Biersay? That's all?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please -- oh, no, we have to ask for the pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] That's tab 1 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecutor, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you. 65 ter 6348.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, because of the protective measures of pseudonym, we will not mention your name in court and we will show you now on the screen a sheet with your details, name and date of birth. Could you please check whether these are correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, then, you are about to -- to make the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. That means that you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury should you give misleading or untruthful information to the Tribunal. Is that understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you then now make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Now, Mr. Registrar, can we have an exhibit number for the pseudonym sheet, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 6348 shall be assigned Exhibit Number P303. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Your witness, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And I take that would be under seal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'll be referring to you by your pseudonym number, which is GH-095, or as "Mr. Witness" because you're protected. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell the Trial Chamber where you were born?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: I was born in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where were you raised?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: In Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where were you educated?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: In Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And where have you lived for most of your life?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: In Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Trial Chamber the ethnic composition of Lovas in early 1991.

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: It had a majority Croatian population. There were some Serbs and some Hungarians as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And which number was greater, the number of Serbs or the number of Hungarians?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe before 1991 what the relationship was between the different ethnicities in your community in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: The relationship was good. We lived together. We socialised. There were no incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how would you describe the atmosphere in Lovas village? Actually ...

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: The atmosphere was friendly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where did you work at the time, the beginning of 1991?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: I worked at the Borovo company.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: It was a leather and footwear factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how many people did it employ?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: Around 20.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how would you describe the ethnic mix of the people who worked there?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: There were people of all ethnicities, from all of the former Yugoslavia. Croats, Serbs, Macedonians.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, how -- could you describe how far is Lovas from the Croatia-Serbian border?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: About 3 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how far is Lovas from Tovarnik?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: 7 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How far from Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: About 30 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The factory that you just described, Borovo, where was that located?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: Between Vukovar and Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay, could the witness please confirm the number of people working in the Borovo factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: About 20.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when you say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: -- 20.000, do you mean in one -- in one place or did they have multiple locations?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: Most of them were in Borovo where I worked, but the factory also had outlets and shops and small work-shops all over Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And the number you gave the Trial Chamber of 20.000, what location were those people working?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: In Borovo itself, in the factory there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You described that the -- the atmosphere in Lovas was good and friendly. Did that begin to change in 1991?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: In the month of May, after the incident in Borovo Selo, things started changing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how -- how were things changing in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: People started mounting guards around the village, and little by little, panic started creeping in. We were close to the border. We saw on TV what had happened in Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what is your understanding of what happened in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: The Croatian police were attacked and killed in that village.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd now like to direct your attention to the end of September 1991. At that time, do you recall hearing shots in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: Not in Lovas. Tanks opened fire from the direction of Tovarnik, in the direction of the local Catholic church.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And where were you when you heard the shots?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: I was in an orchard outside of the village. We were picking apples.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Which village?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: Outside of the village of Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you describe to the Trial Chamber exactly what you heard.

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: We heard shots being fired, and we heard the whistle of the shells. We also heard the noise of the tank engines. When we returned to the village, we saw that the bell-tower of the Catholic church was damaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: On that occasion, were there any shots fired from Lovas itself?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: After this -- what you describe as the damage to the -- to the bell-tower of the Catholic church, was there some indication of what had caused that damage to the Catholic church?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: I didn't know why fire had been opened. There had been no prior provocations. Those columns of tanks were passing from Sid towards Vukovar, and they were not provoked in any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to now move your attention from that first attack on Lovas to what happened in Lovas because of events in Tovarnik. Did there come a time that you learned that Tovarnik had been attacked?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: Yes. One morning, we heard people coming from Tovarnik, from the surrounding places. They were fleeing. They said that tanks had entered the village, opened fire on Croatian houses. They had set fire to the Catholic church, and then they came to the place. They were panicking. We found accommodation for them in houses, if they had friends or relatives.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now you said you heard from people coming from Tovarnik. What ethnicity did these people have?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: They were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you said that: "They had set fire to the Catholic church ..." Who is the "they"? Who set fire to the Catholic church?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: Well, the army that entered the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And which village are we talking about, in this instance?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: Tovarnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You described that accommodation was found for those Croats fleeing Tovarnik. Did you house any of these refugees?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what was the effect on the people of Lovas when they heard the news of what was happening in Tovarnik?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: Well, panic spread. People were afraid because, according to what these Croats who had come from Tovarnik said, there had been people who were killed. Houses had been set on fire. So panic spread amongst them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did something else happen to the Catholic church after the first damage that you described?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: Several days later, after the fall of Tovarnik, a column of tanks that went from Sid to Vukovar fired on the church again. The belfry caught fire and the silos of the agricultural co-operative were also fired on at the entrance to the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Can you estimate how many shells fell on Lovas in this event?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: About four or five.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And did you see the tanks?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: We saw the tanks on the road in the main place.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you recall the first time in 1991 that you saw a JNA officer in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: It was a few days prior to the attack on Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you briefly describe that event to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: Well, when the people arrived from Tovarnik, the inhabitants of our village took a decision. Two Serbs and two Croats went to Sid to speak to the army. They returned and they said they were asking for about a hundred automatic weapons to be handed over, but they weren't in the village. But things remained as they were. Then on the second day, a JNA officer, a driver and a Catholic priest from Tovarnik came and he shouted and said we had to surrender weapons if we didn't want to suffer the same fate as Tovarnik, and he was very angry. He got into his car and then left.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And who said this? Who said -- who shouted and said --

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: The JNA officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: After this ultimatum from the JNA officer, I'd like to direct your attention to the 10th of October, 1991. What happened that morning?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: Well, at about 7.00 in the morning, we heard some explosions. Tank explosions. We hid in the cellar. The explosions stopped a few minutes later. Then they were silent for a few minutes, and then from the direction of Opatovac, you could hear bursts of infantry fire as they were approaching the village, the centre. We hid in the cellars. I live in the centre so I looked out of the window and I saw that from the direction of Opatovac there were armed men approaching and they were driving away the Croats in the street. They knocked on my gate after a while, asked me to come out. They said that they would throw a grenade into the cellar. I came out, opened the door. These were inhabitants of Serbian ethnicity of ours. They started cursing our Ustasha mothers there and so on and so forth. They asked for weapons. I said I didn't have any. They said they would search the house, and then one Serb asked me whether I had any weapons. I said that I didn't. They moved on. He said I should put a white rag or sheet on the gate and remain in the yard. He said I should not go outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Let's slow down just a little bit.

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you heard the fire, you described that "we hid in the cellar." So who -- who hid in the cellar?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: My family. My children. My mother. My wife. There were other neighbours and two elderly Croats from Tovarnik who were with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you described that "they knocked on my gate." Who knocked on your gate?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: The Serbs. Serbian inhabitants of our village and there were some unknown men, and there were Serbs from the village, from Borovo. Serbs I knew from Borovo where we worked together.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe the -- the names -- or give the names of the people who you recognised in that group.

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: Zeljko Krnjaic, Milorad Vorkapic, Milan Vorkapic aka Trnda, Milenko Rudic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you slow down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A Serb from Borovo Selo, Rakic, I knew him because he worked with me in Borovo. And there were unknown persons who weren't from the village and whom I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, you said that they -- they asked for weapons. Did any one in particular ask you for weapons or did they all ask you for weapons?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: Zeljko Krnjaic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Who told you to -- as you say, to put a white sheet or rag on the gate?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: Yes. Dusan Grkovic, a Serb from Lovas, who was in that group.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where did they go after they left your house; do you know?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: They continued down the street towards the machine work-shop of the agricultural co-operative.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is that also known as the -- the work-shop of the Zadruga?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: Yes, the machine work-shop, Zadruga.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What was your understanding about the reason why you had to put a white sheet on your house?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: Well, to show that it was a Croatian house and that it had been searched.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How many of the Croat houses in Lovas had to display a white sheet at this time?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: All the Croatian houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how many Serb houses had to display the white sheet at this time?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: None of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to just step back a little bit. You described that they asked you to open the gate and you did; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you opened the gate to let them in, what, if anything, did you see outside?

utterances.speaker: GH-095
